newsitem.title: PUERTO RICO: Puerto Rico braces for Hurricane Hortense.
newsitem.headline: Puerto Rico braces for Hurricane Hortense.

text.p: Schools and government offices were closed in the U.S. Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico on Monday as Hurricane Hortense slowly carried its 80 mph (130 kph) winds and heavy rains through the northeastern Caribbean.

At 11 a.m. EDT (1500 GMT), Hortense's centre was about 135 miles (220 km) southeast of Ponce, Puerto Rico's second-largest city, near latitude 16.4 north and longitude 65.3 west, and moving west at six mph (nine kph), the National Hurricane Centre said.

A hurricane warning was in effect for Puerto Rico and a tropical storm warning for the U.S. and British Virgin Islands. The government of the Dominican Republic -- the next nation in Hortense's path -- has posted a hurricane watch for parts of its south coast.

In Puerto Rico, supermarkets were busy on Monday as residents stocked up in advance of Hortense. The Puerto Rico Civil Defence prepared to open 300 shelters, Police leave was cancelled and the entire force was put on 24-hour alert.
Gov. Pedro Rossello banned the sale of alcohol, ordered public schools closed and gave the government the day off, save for 600 who were part of an emergency contingency plan.
Schools and government offices also were closed in the U.S. Virgin Islands. But most residents went about business as usual as the storm was expected to pass to the south.
Watches are posted when hurricane or tropical storm conditions are expected within 36 hours. A warning indicates the arrival of such conditions within 24 hours.

Hortense's maximum sustained winds had risen to near 80 mph (130 kph) by midday, making the storm a relatively low Category 1 hurricane. "It had started dying out yesterday morning, and then all of a sudden it started back up again," said National Hurricane Centre meteorologist Trisha Wallace.

forecasters said Hortense was likely to strengthen over the next 24 hours and warned that heavy rains of up to 12 inches (30 cm) could trigger deadly mudslides and flash floods. Some 2,000 people were killed by mudslides and flooding in Haiti, west of the Dominican Republic on Hispaniola island, when Tropical Storm Gordon struck in 1994.

Forecasters also said Hortense could bring storm surge flooding to Puerto Rico's southern coast. Hurricane-force winds extended up to 60 miles (95 km) from Hortense's centre and tropical storm force winds spread 175 miles (280 km).

It was too early for forecasters to predict whether Hortense might threaten the mainland United States as it moved slowly west, hundreds of miles (kilometres) from Florida. "It's entirely too early to tell," Wallace said.

Hurricane Bertha threatened Puerto Rico in early July but passed by, causing at least one drowning death but little damage before heading north toward the U.S. East Coast and making landfall in North Carolina.
